metaDescription: Four plug-in power failure flashlights compared: they charge in the wall, light up when the power cuts out, and lift out to carry through a dark house.
introParagraphs: A power failure flashlight lives in a wall outlet, stays charged, and switches itself on when the household power drops. Pull it out of the socket and it is a regular handheld light. The idea solves the oldest problem with flashlights, which is that they are never where you need them and their batteries are never charged when the lights go out. Here the flashlight is already on the wall, already glowing, and already ready to carry.

This guide covers the four distinct products that truly fit that description. The Energizer Auto-On is sold in several pack sizes, and we treat it as one product. The ROSSEX 4 in 1 uses a built-in lithium battery and doubles as a night light. The Grinsvalley rechargeable light is a compact 60 lumen unit, and the Amerelle LED is a triple-function design with a stated 7 hours of run time per charge. Several other listings repeat these same products in different pack counts, which is why the lineup is four rather than six.

We evaluated each product from its listing specs and typical buyer feedback, so runtime and brightness figures are the makers' claims. The sections below explain how the four differ, which suits which room, and how to combine them with a lantern or bulb for outages that last longer than an evening. Think of this list as the short answer to a common question: which plug-in flashlight should be on my wall.

products.name: Energizer Auto-On LED Flashlights, Rechargeable
products.description:
The Energizer Auto-On is the cleanest, most recognizable version of the idea. The WeatheReady compact LED flashlight plugs into any outlet, charges there, and switches on automatically the moment the power goes out. Lifting it from the wall turns it into a handheld flashlight. The six pack listing describes it as a 40 lumen compact light with a beam reaching up to 30 meters and a run time of up to 3 hours.

Those numbers explain the role it plays. Forty lumens is plenty to cross a room, climb a staircase or check the fuse panel, but three hours is a short window for a long outage. That is the main tradeoff: the Energizer is a first responder, not an all-evening lamp. It is excellent for the first few minutes, when you most need an obvious, automatic light.

The pack sizes matter. A single unit suits an apartment, three cover a bedroom, a hall and a kitchen, and six cover a whole home or a family with grown children. Compared with the ROSSEX, the Energizer is simpler and its pack counts are easier to scale. The listing also suggests keeping one near the door for outdoor use, which is sensible in a storm. A good setup for a two-story home is one on each landing, one in the kitchen and one by the front door. Because the pack sizes scale, you can start with three and add more the first time a storm shows you a dark spot. Remember to wipe the contacts with a dry cloth if a unit ever refuses to charge. The six pack listing also notes uses for work outages and emergency supplies, which makes it handy for a small office.
products.bestFor: Anyone who wants a recognizable brand and an automatic light in each key spot.
pros: 40 lumen output with a long beam
Sold in several convenient pack sizes
cons: Stated run time is only up to 3 hours
Plug-in design uses up an outlet

products.name: ROSSEX 4 in 1 Emergency Flashlights, Plug in Wall
products.description:
The ROSSEX 4 in 1 is the multi-tool of the group. Its listing says it turns on automatically during an outage, charges quickly from any standard socket via a built-in lithium battery, and doubles as a standard flashlight and a night light. The bonus modes mean the same unit can sit in a hallway all year as a gentle glow and still do its emergency job.

The feature that makes it stand out is the choice of pack size. Three, four or six units let you scale to your home, and a larger pack suits a family where each member wants a light at the bedside. The listing does not publish lumen or runtime figures, so we do not state any, and you should test a unit by leaving it unplugged for a while.

Compared with the Energizer, the ROSSEX adds the night light mode but gives fewer published specifications. Compared with the Amerelle, it is more portable but has no stated seven-hour run time. For households that want a flexible, multi-pack set that works as a night light too, the ROSSEX is a thoughtful choice. Place the lights where they will be seen so they are easy to grab. The six pack is a practical choice if you also want lights in a garage, a basement and a workshop. Since the units are identical, a family member can recognize and use any of them without being shown. Pull one out at night every few months to confirm that it lights and holds its glow.
products.bestFor: Families who want one light per bedroom that doubles as a night light.
pros: Night light mode in addition to flashlight
cons: Battery capacity will fade with age

products.name: Grinsvalley Rechargeable Emergency Light, 60 Lumen
products.description:
The Grinsvalley light states 60 lumens, which is the highest published figure in this lineup and above the Energizer's 40 lumen claim. It recharges while plugged into the wall, switches on automatically at an outage and works as a night light, emergency light and flashlight.

Sixty lumens of output means it can light a room more fully than a 40 lumen unit, while still being small enough to tuck beside a bed. The pack sizes of two or three units suit smaller homes. The listing describes the unit as a power failure night light that instantly switches to a bright emergency mode.

The drawback is that the maker does not publish a runtime, so you have to test it yourself. Compared with the Amerelle, which claims seven hours, it is smaller and more flexible, but it gives you less certainty. It is a good fit for an apartment where two lights cover the whole route from the bedroom to the front door. Because this light is sold as a pair or a trio, it also works as an easy gift for a parent who lives alone. Place one beside the bed and one in the bathroom, and the dangerous late-night route is covered. If the silver finish is visible against a pale wall, it is also easy to spot in the dark.
products.bestFor: Apartments and small homes that want a bright light from just two or three units.
cons: Only two or three units per pack

products.name: Amerelle LED Emergency Lights, Triple Function
specs: Power failure light, flashlight and night light
products.description:
The Amerelle is the pick for people who worry most about runtime. The listing says a fully charged unit lasts 7 hours, which is more than double the Energizer's stated 3 hours. It is described as a triple-function light that serves as a plug-in emergency light, a power failure flashlight and a night light, with a front panel that lights up automatically when the power fails.

That longer window changes how you use it. Instead of treating it as a quick escape light, you can let it glow through an evening without worrying that it will fade within a couple of hours. Install them around the home so each room has one, and move the one nearest to you as you go.

The tradeoff is that the listing does not publish a brightness figure, so you cannot compare lumens with the Energizer or Grinsvalley. As with all of these, runtime is the maker's claim and will shorten with battery age. If you want a plug-in flashlight to last through an evening, the Amerelle is the best match here. If a family member visits and needs the guest room covered, move one from the kitchen for the night. Since the front panel lights up automatically when power fails, you will notice an outage even from another room. Keep a lantern nearby for the hours after the seven are over.
products.bestFor: Evening outages where a light needs to last several hours.
pros: Longest stated run time at 7 hours

buyingCriteria.explanation: This is the clearest difference in the group. The Amerelle states 7 hours, while the Energizer states up to 3 hours. The ROSSEX and Grinsvalley do not publish a figure. A short run time is enough to escape or reach a lantern, but not to see you through an evening. Pair short-run flashlights with a longer-lasting lantern or bulb. A simple rule is to write the run time next to the light on a sticky note, so you remember how long you have. Plan your evening around the shortest claim in the home.

Published output is limited. The Energizer lists 40 lumens and the Grinsvalley lists 60 lumens, while the ROSSEX and Amerelle give no figure. Roughly 20 to 40 lumens is enough for a hallway, and about 80 lumens lights a room. When a listing is silent, assume a modest output and treat the flashlight as a path light. Even a modest light is useful when your eyes have adjusted to the dark, which takes several minutes. Resist the urge to flick the brightest setting on at once.

Count the spots where a fall would be worst: bedside, bathroom, top and bottom of the stairs, and the kitchen. The Energizer comes in 1, 3 and 6 pack counts, the ROSSEX in 3, 4 and 6, and the Grinsvalley in 2 and 3. Buy enough units that none of your key paths is left dark. It is better to have too many than too few. Think in routes rather than rooms. A route from the bed to the bathroom to the kitchen needs a light roughly every ten feet if the hall is long.

These lights lift out of the wall and must be comfortable in the hand. Look at the size, the grip surface and whether the switch is easy to find. A compact Energizer is easy to hold in one hand. A bulkier unit may be harder to carry for someone with a weak grip. Hold the unit in each hand and check that you can lift it out of the wall without a twist or a pinch. If it is awkward in a store or at home, it will be worse in the dark.

Night light and tabletop modes add value if you want one device to do several jobs. The ROSSEX and Amerelle both include night light functions. Extra modes also add small complexity, so decide whether you want them. A simple on and off device can be easier to live with. If you only want a flashlight, choose the plainest design. If you want a night light too, accept that more modes mean slightly more to learn.

Built-in batteries fade over several years. The ROSSEX uses a lithium cell, and all four types are rechargeable. Test each light twice a year by unplugging it for an hour. Replace any that no longer holds a charge for a reasonable time. Mark the first test date on a calendar, and repeat in six months. A light that has been left in a hot room will age faster, so avoid outlets above radiators.

faq.q: How is a power failure flashlight different from a regular flashlight?
faq.a: It stays plugged into a wall outlet and charges there. When the power fails, it turns on automatically. You can then lift it out and carry it. It is the same idea as an emergency flashlight kept in a kitchen drawer, only the wall holds it for you. For older adults it removes the hardest step of an outage, which is finding a light before you can move safely.

faq.q: How long does the light last?
faq.a: It varies. The Energizer states up to 3 hours and the Amerelle states 7 hours. The ROSSEX and Grinsvalley do not publish a runtime. If you need longer, add a lantern.

faq.q: Why are there only four picks?
faq.a: Many listings are the same unit sold in different pack counts. We counted each product once and chose not to pad the list with other items. That left four distinct picks. We did not want to repeat the same unit under different names.

The Energizer lists 40 lumens and the Grinsvalley 60 lumens, which is enough to walk a hallway or a staircase. They do not light a whole room for long. Pair them with a lantern. They are meant for the first hours. Remember that lumens only tell part of the story, because a wider beam makes a room feel better lit than a narrow one with the same number.

faq.q: How often should I test them?
faq.a: Twice a year, unplug a unit and check that it lights for several minutes. Replace any that fade quickly. Built-in batteries wear with age. Keep a note of the date.

faq.q: Do I need one in every room?
faq.a: Cover the bedroom, bathroom, stairs and kitchen. Larger homes need more. Pack sizes of three or four are a good start. Add more if the house is large. Put the first light where you step out of bed and the second in the bathroom.
